title: Amazing Grace
composer: Traditional hymn tune “New Britain” (words by John Newton)
about: A Southern hymn that bluegrass banjo players learn early. The melody note falls on the beat, and the roll fills the space between with open strings that ring, often with the short 5th string. Play the melody notes a little louder than the roll notes. The letters under the tab are the picking fingers
source: The melody is the one in our piano arrangement of Amazing Grace, which was checked note by note against the Mutopia Project’s “New Britain” hymn setting (public domain); here it sounds an octave lower, as it does on the banjo, with roll notes added between the melody notes. Our checking script compares the two melodies beat by beat.

title: Amazing Grace
composer: Traditional hymn tune “New Britain” (words by John Newton)

title: Amazing Grace
composer: Traditional hymn tune “New Britain” (words by John Newton)
about: Count three beats in each bar. The tune starts with one pickup note on beat 3, before the first full bar. In bar 7 the melody climbs to the D above the staff: move your right hand up for it, and back down in bar 10.

title: Boil Them Cabbage Down (clawhammer)
about: A cheerful old-time song about a simple supper, and one of the first tunes most banjo players learn. title: Canon in D
about: The left hand plays the same eight bass notes over and over, two bars at a time, just as the cello does in Pachelbel’s piece. Learn that pattern first: it never changes. Then add the right hand, which plays the first violin part: slow notes at first, then flowing eighth notes.
source: Notes checked note by note against the score of the opening on Wikipedia’s “Pachelbel’s Canon” page (violin I and cello). We keep those two lines for bars 1 to 10 and add a final D chord.

title: Dry Creek Blues
about: In the early country blues the thumb is the drummer: it plays a steady beat on the open bass string of the chord (E, A or the B on the 5th string) and never stops, while the fingers play short answering phrases on the top strings. title: Durang’s Hornpipe
composer: Attributed to Mr. Hoffmaster, John Durang’s violin teacher (about 1785); long since a traditional fiddle tune
about: One of the oldest American fiddle tunes with a known story: Durang’s violin teacher wrote it for him around 1785, early in his career as a dancer, and it has been played for dancing ever since. With a capo at the 2nd fret, double C tuning becomes a D A D E (raise the 5th string to A, or use a spike)
source: Melody checked note by note against “Durang’s Hornpipe” in Cole’s 1000 Fiddle Tunes (the 1940 reissue of Ryan’s Mammoth Collection, 1883), as transcribed in ABC by Bob Puckette at MIT’s abc collection (trillian.mit.edu). title: Gymnopédie No. 1
about: Satie marked it “Lent et douloureux”: slow and sorrowful. In every bar the left hand plays a low bass note and then a soft chord in the middle of the keyboard. The melody floats above with long held notes. The opening chords rock gently between G major 7 and D major 7.

title: Hot Cross Buns
about: Three notes and three fingers. Put your right thumb on middle C, finger 2 on D and finger 3 on E, and leave them there the whole time. In bar 3 the notes go twice as fast: these are eighth notes, two to each beat.

title: Prelude in E minor
about: Chopin marked this prelude Largo: very slow. The right hand sings just a few notes, often only B and C, while the left-hand chords sink one half step at a time. Listen to how each new chord changes only one note. The music swells in the middle, then fades into silence before the last chords.
source: Mutopia Project edition (Magnus Lewis-Smith, from the Peters edition, 1879; public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script. A turn and two grace notes in that edition are left out. The half-step motion is described in Wikipedia’s article on the prelude.

title: Prelude in E Minor
about: A rippling study over the open low E string. Count two big beats in each bar, each split into six quick notes: thumb on the bass, then the fingers climb to the top string and come back down. source: Mutopia Project edition of Carcassi’s Preludes in Progressive Keys, Op. 59 (entered by Jeffrey Olson from the 1906 Oliver Ditson edition by G. C. Santisteban; public domain). Upper and lower voices read twice and compared with this file note by note.

title: Sonatina in C major, first movement
about: A sonatina is a short sonata, and this is one of the first that piano students learn. Listen for the opening tune: it comes back near the end, an octave lower. Count two half-note beats in each bar (cut time) and keep the scales even.
source: Mutopia Project edition (Brian D. Rude, from the G. Schirmer Sonatina Album, 1893; public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script. That edition prints no dynamics in this movement, only the word Spiritoso. Date from Wikipedia.

title: The Entertainer (opening)
about: Ragtime sets a steady, march-like left hand against a right hand that lands just off the beat. The left hand jumps: a low bass note on the beat, then a chord in the middle of the keyboard. Practice the left hand alone until the jumps feel easy. Joplin wrote “Not fast” at the top.

title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star
composer: Traditional (French tune, 1761; words by Jane Taylor, 1806)
about: The first piece for both hands. The left hand plays one slow note while the right hand sings the tune. Play each hand alone first, then put them together slowly. In the first line your right hand sits a little higher: thumb on C, finger 4 on G and finger 5 on A.
source: Melody checked against the theme of Mozart’s Variations on “Ah vous dirai-je, maman”, K. 265 (Mutopia Project edition for two guitars, from the Porro print; public domain). The notes match. Mozart repeats the note on the long words (“star”, “are”) and adds two small decorations (bars 7 and 15); the song as sung holds a half note there instead. Dates from Wikipedia.

title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star
